utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask the Court if this witness could be given a Rule 90(E) warning, and I understand his protective measures have been announced but he is a witness who has a pseudonym and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To enable the witness to enter the courtroom, we go into closed session.

utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again, welcome to the courtroom, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. Like in the last trial when you were present as a witness, there are protective measures in place for you. You will be addressed by a pseudonym and nobody outside the courtroom will recognise you by face. On the request of the Prosecution, I would like to caution you. I quote: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent Prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Did you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin, your examination in chief, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, witness. As you know my name is Rupert Elderkin, before we get started just like to ask you to speak slowly and leave a pause as necessary for the interpreters to keep up with your answers. And if there's anything that I ask you that's unclear, then please let me know and I'll do my best to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 7206. And that should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, without saying aloud what is written on the screen, please can you confirm if that is your name?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to ask for the pseudonym sheet to be admitted under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 07206, the pseudonym sheet would be assigned P01942 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall testifying at this Tribunal during the course of two days in April of 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review that testimony recently?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Does your testimony fairly and accurately reflect what you would say if you were to be examined here today and if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was all correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd at this point ask to have the witness's prior testimony admitted, and that's 65 ter numbers 6634 which is the confidential testimony under seal, and 6635, the public transcript, along with the associated exhibits which were indicated in the exhibit list for this witness. And if necessary I can read out their 65 ter numbers as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We'll start with the two transcripts, they will be received. The first one 6634 under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, would be assigned P01943 under seal. And the other transcript under 65 ter number 06635 would be assigned P01944.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we turn to the five documents previously admitted in the previous trial. 6636 through 6679, they will be received as well, the first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 06636 would be assigned P01945 under seal, 65 ter number 03380 would be assigned P01946. 65 ter number 06637 will be assigned P01947, 65 ter number 03379 will be assigned P01948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I may now read a short summary of the witness's evidence, and this can remain in open session. The witness, who is of Serb ethnicity, was a member of the VRS Zvornik Brigade's Military Police Company in 1995. The company commander was Lieutenant Miomir Jasikovac. One day in July 1995, the witness was on duty at the Sepak border crossing. At around 11.00 a.m. he received a telephone call from Lieutenant Jasikovac to go to Rocevic. He went there in a private vehicle and found two or three of his colleagues already there. He was told to set up a check-point on the road leading towards the school, to check passing vehicles and keep civilians away. When the witness arrived, there was a group of around 20 to 30 Serb civilians, who the witness kept away from the school. There were other soldiers at the school, where a group of Muslim prisoners from Srebrenica were being held. The Serb civilians were swearing and shouting. They wanted to enter the school for revenge. While the witness was at the check-point a couple of vehicles passed by, coming from the direction of the main road. One of the cars stopped. The witness heard later that the Zvornik Brigade security officers Drago Nikolic and Trbic (presumably Captain Milorad Trbic) had come and told the soldiers that everything must be kept under control. The witness did not personally see Drago Nikolic, but he did see Trbic across from the check-point in the school-yard. The witness left Rocevic at around 1700 hours. Later, at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, at around 1830 hours, the witness saw some people upstairs wearing camouflage uniforms. He asked who they were and was told, "Well, the commander has a meeting with Popovic and Beara." While the witness and his colleagues were talking, Lieutenant Jasikovac was present and he said, "What do you need to know who is up there? None of your business." And told them to quieten down. The witness saw that Popovic had a mustache, but he did not see Beara. The witness only went to Rocevic on one day in July 1995. He believes that the date was the 11th of July. Your Honours, I'd like to ask the witness now a few additional questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, please tell us who was the Military Police Company administrative clerk in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: You are asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: All right. Now, I don't know whether he was the non-commissioned officer or what, but it was Stevo Kostic, he was the officer of the the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like, please, to have Exhibit P1754 on the screen. And that should not be broadcast. And if we could go to the second page of this document. Or in fact, sorry, page 3 even, in e-court. The second page is a blank page. And if possible, if we could zoom in on the top left-hand corner of that, just so we can see the names more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Well, this is the daily log of the presence at duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could just scroll across to the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us for what period is this the daily log?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: It says July 1995 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask at this time if the witness could be shown the original of the document. A lot of the markings on the paper are in pencil and they are much easier to see in the original. Also offer that at this time if the Defence, or also Your Honours, would like to scrutinise the document. I've, indeed, also brought a magnifying-glass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be given to the Defence first with the assistance of the court usher, and then to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, for your information there is an English translation of this document in e-court but after the first page where it comprises just a list of names, then I'm not sure that it would assist. It maybe easier simply to have the B/C/S on screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please turn to the page of the document which I've marked with the sticker number 1, so I think it should be the second of the pages in front of you. And that should now be the same as the page which we had on the screen a moment ago. Sir, do you see your company commander's name on this list?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Tell us where it appears on the list, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I actually only wanted for the list to be moved on the screen but now it was already done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, please, where your company commander's name appears on this list?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: It's number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you also just mentioned a moment ago Stevo Kostic as the company's administrative clerk. Can you tell us, please, if you see his name on this list?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: It's number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you please now look across the line of markings to the right of the company commander Miomir Jasikovac. So underneath the numbers we have there 1, 2, 3, 4, et cetera. And I'd like to ask you to look carefully, please, at the entry under the date for the 15th. Can you tell us, first of all, what is marked there under the 15th for Jasikovac?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: I see a letter T, but what it means I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now looking carefully, can you see if something was written there before the T was put on? If you need to use the magnifying-glass, please do so as well.

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: I can see R in Latin alphabet or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we now please have page 7 of the document in e-court on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And for you, sir, that would be the sticker number 2 that is marked on the copy you have in front of you. So again without reading it out loud, can you see your name on this page?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us which number of the list it appears at, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, could you now look across at the entries written across to the right of your name. First of all, could you tell us what are the entries indicated for your name between the 1st and the 11th?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: I think it's number 6 but I wouldn't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Then, sir, after the 11th, could you just tell us what are the next few entries for your name?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Letter T, just as the others that you can see above.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you see the letter T for the entries under 12, 13, 14 and 15?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, could you look closely please at the entry under 15 against your name, and can you see if something was written there before? Again, please feel free to use the magnifying-glass if necessary.

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: It's similar. It's similar to other corrections. It seems that there may have been an R there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we now please see the next page in e-court, page 8. And this time it might help to have the English translation alongside if that's possible, and that would be page 5 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, sir, that's the back of the page that you are looking at if you just turn over that page. Mr. Witness, if you turn over the page in front of you. And there you should see some pencil writing on the left-hand side of the sheet. Sir, you've just identified some of the markings that were beside your name including the number 6 and the letter T, can you see from this page what those letters mean on the log?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: It probably means that he, the administrative clerk, used some sort of abbreviations in order for to know who was there or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you see what the abbreviation T represents according to this page in front of us?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Some sort of a field duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how about the number 6?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't be able to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the word "batagoni" next to a large bracket about halfway down the list?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can you tell what it says to the left of that, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: It's numbers from 1 to 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, can you see beneath the letter T for "teren" what appears to be a blank space on the list? Underneath the T, "teren," and then if you look beneath that you see TZ, "teren Zepa." Between "teren" and "teren Zepa" do you see a blank line?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Yes, there is a bit more space here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd ask you again, please, to look carefully at that space, if necessary with a magnifying-glass, and see whether you can identify anything that was previously written in that space?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Well, it looks something like O, and then there's a dash, and then Orahovici or Orahovica or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Anywhere on this list that you can see what the code letter R represented?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Well, I can't see it on this page, there is no R.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know what it represented?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Well, I can't really speculate. I don't know what this administrative officer meant by it, administrative clerk. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could it mean Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Well, it's possible. It could. But it doesn't appear on the list anywhere whereas we see that all the other field duties do appear on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, could you please take a moment to look through the three pages, so the back, the other side of the page you are currently looking at, and the other two pages which have names on them and see if you recognise the names of any of your colleagues who were with you the day in July of 1995 when you were on duty at Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Well, there are a lot of names here and it's really hard to remember each one of them here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you see any of the following MPs while you were on duty at Rocevic. First, Dragoje Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: I can't recall. I really can't recall the first names of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How about Predrag Ristic?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Well, that name is completely unfamiliar. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How about Zeljko Stevanovic, was he with you the day you were at Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Well, anything I say now I could go wrong. I really can't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If I may, I'd just like to say the last names as well, Milomir Simic, Stanoje Bucakovic, Sladjan Jokic, were any of those men with you or were they -- any of those men at Rocevic the day you were there?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: Probably they were. There were some other three men but I can't really recall their names, so I can't tell you specifically whether they were the ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, did you see Lieutenant Jasikovac while you were on duty that day at Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: PW-059
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we go into private session, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honours, and witness, that concludes my examination-in-chief. I don't have any further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, now it's your time for commencing the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this house for all those present and may God's will be done in these proceedings, and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish. And I also would like to wish a safe journey home to this witness, and just to add that I have no questions for this witness in view of the fact that Mr. Elderkin explored all the issues that I would have explored. Thank you, Mr. President. I am done with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin, there's no room for re-examination, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Based on the absence of any cross-examination, Your Honours, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, surprisingly early, you will be pleased to realise that this concludes your examination here in the courtroom. Thank you very much that you came to The Hague again and to provide us with your knowledge. Now you are free to return to your normal activity and the court usher will assist you. We go into closed session to enable you to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that the next witness is currently being brought over from his hotel so unfortunately he is not able to start immediately, and I would ask whether we might be able to take a break now, that's enough time for him to get here, and also given the slightly more cramped surroundings, it might make the change-over for the Prosecution team slightly easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is a reasonable suggestion. What do you think, when can we start again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Would a 20 minute break be possible, and then I understand that should be fine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it would be reasonable to have the normal first break now and we will resume at half past 3.00, then we will manage to finish at 7.00 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Thayer. Welcome to the courtroom. Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon to Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Defence, everyone in the courtroom. Yes, the witness is ready. We snatched him from the hotel to bring him over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please read the solemn declaration on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Thayer for the Prosecution has questions for you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could you please just state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Edward Paul Joseph. My last name is Joseph.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying in this building for a little over two days in August of 2007?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you recently read that testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you attest that the transcript that you read accurately reflected what you said during that testimony in that prior case, the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We speak the same language, so I'll try to slow down a little bit first and also we need to leave a pause between my questions and your answers and I think that will be helpful to everybody. utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I can so attest that my answers would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within -- within the bounds of reason. I can't say that verbatim my words would be a hundred per cent identical, but the meaning, I believe, would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 7194.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned P01949.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is a mistake. It should be 1950. We have received with the last witness the last one ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Everybody told me I was wrong, so it is the correct number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just one small qualification, but these are serious formal proceedings so I want to be very, very precise. utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this additional remark. Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We do have some associated exhibits to tender through this witness, and I will just go through our exhibit list.

utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, to shorten this procedure, we have received this list. Just tell for the record the first and the last 65 ter number, then the Registry will circulate an internal memorandum with the P numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you, there are three documents 65 ter 7204, 7205, and 7208 which are not on the 65 ter exhibit lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, those are non-associated exhibits which we had considered using with the witness during his examination-in-chief today. utterances.text: The Chamber would be in a better position and would appreciate if the Prosecution would not just put a note at the end of the exhibit lists with the leave of the Chamber but would move for an addition to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about a written motion. I'm talking about an oral submission that was sufficient, but just to put a star within a remark is perhaps not the best way to deal with that. Mr. Gajic, I think, is on his feet to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone. Your Honour, I believe that there is a minor problem here, maybe it's an e-court problem or access that the Defence has to e-court. The documents, the 65 ter document 7204, 7205, 7197, 7198, 7199, and a few others that I haven't really had time to check, unfortunately we have no access to these documents in e-court. utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I see an additional problem, Mr. Thayer. In the first document you mentioned in this category is 65 ter 7195, I don't have that on my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the date of the list to which Your Honour's referring. We distributed a list on the 28th of February. It's the first document in that second category of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Turns out that I have -- thank you very much. Yes. Obviously I have a list also of the 28th of March, perhaps a little earlier, or there's something wrong. If that isn't the case, I was shown it and I think you may proceed and -- thank you very much. Now I have the updated list. Can you state if all these documents have a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, it turns out that there are additional problems. I was told by the Registrar that he can't see some of these documents including the transcript in the Popovic case we just received into evidence. It is not accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are trying to fix that now. Second one is 07196 and 07199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gajic, is the Defence in agreement with the addition of these three documents to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've mentioned the fact that we don't have access to e-court in respect of two of these documents. utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think for the moment, we will of course receive the documents admitted through the witness in prior proceeding 65 ter 7195 and then through the whole list to the last one which is 65 ter 2080, but those you have indicated which have no translation yet will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, just so that we can get to work, I can tell you that with respect to those three documents that don't have translations at the moment and with respect to, I think, all but one of the documents which the Defence says it doesn't have access to, I will not be referring to any of those documents during my examination-in-chief and from what I've seen of the Defence list it's not on their list of document, so I don't think these are documents that are going to be at issue in any event, at least the ones that are on the associated exhibit list. With respect to those that didn't have 65 ter numbers, to the extent I was going to possibly use them they are at the end of my direct examination, so I think we can get started, with the Court's permission, with the witness's testimony and we can deal with those other matters later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. And if there are problems, they should be raised and then we will deal with them case by case. The Registry will provide you with P numbers by internal memorandum. Please continue, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do have a 92 ter summary for the witness. In July 1995, the witness was serving in a civilian capacity as a civil affairs officer with UNPROFOR. On or about 12 or 13 July, he was tasked to work with the civil affairs team at the Tuzla airbase where he saw thousands of mostly women from Srebrenica arrive in buses. The women were quite thin, quite distraught, and concerned about the fate of their men. He recalls one woman trying to scale a barbed wire fence with her bare hands because she had heard a rumour that some men from Srebrenica were nearby. The witness stayed in Tuzla for about a week until he and another civil affairs officer, Viktor Bezruchenko were sent to Zepa on 20 July. En route, they passed through a number of VRS check-points, then arrived at OP 2, which was under VRS control. He saw a number of VRS military vehicles and booming loud-speakers set up around the area in support of psychological operations conveying the message that there was no chance for the population. They then saw General Mladic with a representative of UNHCR and of ICRC. They were told to sit down and while lunch was served, a VRS officer filmed the discussions for propaganda purposes. After awhile, firing commenced from VRS cannon positions towards Zepa and they were told to leave. Upon return to Sarajevo, he reported to David Harland at Sector Sarajevo and John Ryan, the senior civil affairs officer. Meetings concerning the fate of Zepa and the related issue of prisoner exchange were held at the Sarajevo airport. From the Muslim side, an "all for all" exchange had to include the missing men from Srebrenica. From the Serb side, the status of the men from Zepa was the concern. The witness and Bezruchenko travelled to Zepa a second time on 25 July. En route, they stopped by the UNHCR offices to discuss UNHCR's decision not to participate in the evacuation of the Zepa population because it did not want to be accused of assisting in ethnic cleansing. They arrived again at OP2 and met with Mladic who told them to go down into Zepa town. They arrived at the Ukrainian compound in the school in Zepa and met with the Muslim leadership, including Hamdija Torlak. UNPROFOR was the only international presence, as ICRC limited its participation to evacuating the wounded. The next day, 26 July, the witness went to the centre of Zepa and saw a concentration of women huddled with their children. Following instruction from the UNHCR, the witness and Bezruchenko began asking the women if they were leaving of their own free will, to which they answered yes. This continued for another 15 to 19 women, until one woman told them that she was not leaving of her own free will and that she wanted to stay but did not know who would protect her. She then began to cry, after which all the women began to cry. The witness's clear impression was that Zepa was their home but that they were terrified as to their fate if they stayed. As soon as the vehicles arrived, the transportations began, which was basically the VRS logistical part of the operation. Vehicles would come down the one-lane dirt road from the steep gorge into Zepa, fill up, turn around and go back up. There were not enough peacekeepers to escort each bus. Separately from this, an UNPROFOR doctor and a VRS doctor with an ICRC representative screened the wounded to see who required evacuation, those deemed seriously wounded were evacuated under French escort. At one point, Muslim women who remained in the centre saw the UNPROFOR convoy leaving, blocked the convoy because they thought it was the last one and were panic-stricken that they would be left behind. During the two full days of evacuations, the witness saw Generals Mladic and Tolimir actively gauging what was going on and supervising. They were the highest ranking VRS officers he saw engaged in the operation. During the transportations, there was a lightly wounded man with his arm in a sling who was acting as a spokesperson for the other lightly wounded and who repeatedly approached the witness and Bezruchenko seeking to be evacuated with the women and children. The witness met with the accused in town and asked him if the lightly wounded could be evacuated with the last bus. The accused agreed, and the lightly wounded boarded the bus. Given that these lightly would you wounded were military-aged men, the witness told the French major to put a peacekeeper on each bus and have an APC follow it. On 27 July, the witness was also present for a meeting between civilian leaders from Zepa and the VRS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. -- at which General Smith was also present. The civilian leaders appeared ready to sign a capitulation agreement on behalf of the Zepa Muslims, but the witness was concerned that they lacked the authority to do so and that any surrender would therefore lack validity, and informed Smith about his concerns. On 27 July, after the last convoy had left, the witness saw two heavily-armed VRS soldiers with aggressive demeanour enter the UNPROFOR compound at the school in Zepa, grab Avdo Palic, and drive away with him. The witness and Bezruchenko attempted to follow in their car, but were unsuccessful. After General Smith left Zepa, the hodza and one or two other Muslims were also taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a couple of questions to follow up on some topics you testified about in the Popovic case and to show you some reports that you were not shown in that case that I think you can help the Trial Chamber with. Now, the first thing I want to ask you about is, you testified in the Popovic case - and this is at transcript page 14170 to -171, for the record - that during the VRS attack on Zepa, both the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Serb forces threatened to kill the Ukrainian peacekeepers. And I think testified that you received information to that effect and we saw that in some memos that were discussed in the last trial. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I do recall that and that is also in the line of where reports were shown to me that refreshed my recollection of that -- of those threats and my awareness of those threats at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at two documents very quickly along those lines. The first one is 65 ter 2154, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what we can see here, sir, is a sitrep, a situation report, here it's called a sync rep by the Ukrainians, we can see it's from UKRBAT and that's Ukrainian battalion; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it's dated the 16th of July, 1995, and I want to turn your -- direct your attention to the portion which begins with the word "Charlie." Do you see that there, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I do. It might be easier for me just to read the English, but if --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure, just -- do you have the English on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I do, but it would be bigger if I only had the English. I don't know if it's possible to do that. But anyway, it's all right. I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the B/C/S we need to go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need both versions on the screen to enable the accused to look at the same document at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. Very well. Maybe if we could blow up, Charlie, if we could maybe enlarge that a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see it, and it states: "Re-establishment communication between base and CP2."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have the English version on the screen. I don't have. Sorry, yes, the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's definitely a Monday, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this reminder.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what the abbreviation "CP2" is?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: CP or OP?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Either one. If it's OP, tell us what OP2 is, and if it's CP, tell us what CP2 is.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Well, OP would be observation post, CP could be check point, but in this context it would be OP2 is what we generally understood the location that was the designation that UNPROFOR had given that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indeed. So observation posts were referred in your experience to as OPs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: That's my understanding, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. As we read on, there's reference to the personnel mounted Defence, the Serbs directed their weapons to the Ukrainian soldiers, and reiterated that if NATO undertakes any actions against them, they will kill the OP or as you read it OP personnel. The question is simple, is this the type of information that you were receiving during this period of time concerning the status of the Ukrainian peacekeepers vis-a-vis the warring parties and how they were being treated?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: In a -- yes, this is the nature, this is the type of information. Whether I was actually shown this report at the time, I cannot say. But we were generally aware of the plight of the Ukrainian battalion second-hand, that is through them. These were not threats that I had received directly from either side there, but to answer your question, yes, this is in the nature of the information that we would have had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, to put it even more simply, do you recall receiving reports that both sides were threatening to kill the Ukrainians?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I think in general we were aware of the difficult situation that they were in, correct, and that there were threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 2154.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, will be assigned P01950.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may have 65 ter 7200 briefly, please. Well, this is one of our problematic ones. I do have a hard copy that we can throw up on the ELMO, and if the Defence needs -- actually, this is one that we don't have a translation for, so if we just throw it up on the ELMO, I think we can look at it the old-fashioned way with the Court Officer's assistance, please. It's a very, very short report, so I can just read it in and the accused will receive the translation that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We can mostly see the document on the screen. The date is 20 July, 1995. It's another Ukrainian battalion sync rep and again next to the entry for "Charlie," I'll just read it into the record, it says: "The commander of Bosnian --" and now I don't have my hard copy so I can't read it on the screen, Bosnian something?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: BDE.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Oh, brigade, BDE. Thank you, Witness. "... BDE in Zepa Avdo Palic announced that if the helicopter with representatives of BHC FWD," and, sir, can you tell us what that abbreviation is, if you know? BHC FWD?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina command forward. Bosnia-Herzegovina command forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember where that was located, that command?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: That command would have been I believe was still -- was then in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: And forward, these are UN designations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right. And then we see the abbreviation UKRBAT-1, UNHCR, UN ICRC and UNMOs doesn't arrive to Zepa by 21, and then we see some hours: 0800 hours, Bravo 1995, Bosnians will kill Ukrainians. Again, the question is the same, sir, is this the type of information that you were receiving concerning the treatment of the peacekeepers by both of the warring factions during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Affirmative. This is in the nature of the information that we were receiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender 65 ter 7200, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be received, pending -- it will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that document will be assigned P01951 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to spend most of the rest of our time together doing, sir, is looking at some reports, numerous examples of which you were shown in the Popovic trial but not these. May I show you one or two from the Popovic trial to ask you some more detail but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by way of explanation for the Trial Chamber, we have uploaded an exhibit from the Popovic case which is a collection of reports from David Harland - and you'll hear a little bit more about David Harland - up the chain of command within the UN concerning the events in Zepa. The Trial Chamber in the last -- in the Popovic trial had asked us to put those into a packet form, which we did in hard copy, and that has been uploaded with tabs in e-court separating the various reports, so it will start with tab 1 and end with tab 18 with a divider sheet in between. We have updated this packet to reflect the current 65 ter numbers. What is currently uploaded into e-court has the Popovic 65 ter numbers, but we'll have a new and improved version with the appropriate P numbers and exhibit numbers as well, which we can distribute to the parties and to the Trial Chamber in hard copy, which will be a little easier, but in the mean time we'll work with e-court as we move through this packet of documents. I just wanted to give you that background so you had an idea of the what we are looking at the on the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And to have it on the record, this is 65 ter 2438; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. And we've also furnished the Defence with a translation of this packet. There are a few translations that are still outstanding, but they have a mirror image in B/C/S to work with as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you spoke briefly in the last trial about David Harland, I think you described his position, and you stated, and this is at transcript page 14164 to -165, that he was quite methodical in reporting and that his reports, and this is at 14217 of the prior transcript, were accurate, contemporaneous recollections of communication that we had, meaning that you and Mr. Harland had. What I'd like to ask you is if you can describe for the Trial Chamber in just a little bit more detail the general nature of your communications with Mr. Harland, and I don't mean the substance at this point, but just how you would communicate, how frequently you would communicate during this period of time, when you went down to Zepa twice, returned to Sarajevo, and were witnessing the events that you witnessed.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I see that Mr. Gajic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only one suggestion, the transcript is literally flying in front of our eyes, so the witness begins his answer before the interpretation of the question is finished. It happens quite often, so I would like to ask both speakers to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And especially not to overlap, that happens always in the courtroom. Please wait with your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not very helpful because we don't receive your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought the interpreters translate everything. My apologies, if they do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But if one speaker is moving from and switching from one language to the other this is technically very complicated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just continue with your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. To answer your question, David Harland and I were long time colleagues, UNPROFOR civil affairs colleagues, in Bosnia, and we had close communication certainly over this period. The nature of the communication changed, of course, depending on whether I was co-located with him in Sarajevo or when Viktor Bezruchenko and I had gone to Zepa, in which case we were dependent on the technical means that existed, such as they did, for us to communicate there. But when we were back in Sarajevo, David and I were in close personal communication and, of course, Viktor and I tried to be dutiful about reporting from Zepa to David as best we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during the period of time when you were physically in Zepa or en route to Zepa, can you tell the Trial Chamber what activities Mr. Harland was engaged in in Sarajevo pertaining to Zepa and what was happening in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: In addition to the reporting that you can see and all those who have the documents can see, the reporting that David was conveying higher up in the UN chain, you can also see that David was playing an important role in communicating with the parties both Serbs and at that time, as it's referred to in the documents, the Bosnian side, that's how it is referred to in that document in those days, and David in particular was present for these negotiations about a prisoner exchange. So he was, in Sarajevo, was performing an important role both in reporting and also in maintaining communication with the interlocutors from the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it fair to refer to those meetings in Sarajevo about the prisoner exchange as the airport meetings, as a shorthand way of referring to them, because that's where they were occurring? Is that fair to do?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: You could refer to them in that way. I would just say be advised that prior to and subsequent to, there may have been other meetings at the airport. The airport was the traditional location for such meetings being accessible to both Serbs and the Bosnian side in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how would you describe the flow of information between you and Mr. Harland during this period of time, let's focus right now on when you were physically on the ground in Zepa and he was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: It's hard for me to be absolutely precise about the flow. We -- Viktor and I did the best we could to provide information and to stay in some kind of communication, but we were under - and I would emphasise this to all those concerned here - we were under tremendous stress and there was an enormous operation that we had to be physically present for, so -- and also I would call attention to the fact that in those days, this is pre-Internet, pre-e-mail, pre all of that, so it was voice communication at that time. We didn't even have ability to send a fax from Zepa. So we tried and did what we could to maintain, to communicate essential matters, but the flow was somewhat intermittent because of the operational conditions we were working under in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what kind of communications means did you use when you were in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Once -- I'm pausing here with respect for interpretation. With -- once the French units had arrived, I recall that they had in their APC that they had means that we used, whether they were radio or radio telephone at this point, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you and Mr. Bezruchenko were under tremendous stress. What was the source and nature of that stress that you are speaking about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: This was a -- this was a very challenging, which is a word that barely describes it. This was a very difficult and -- operation with -- in which we had responsibility and were aware of the potential for loss of life and also the potential for crimes to occur such as rapes and other potential risk. So Viktor and I were under -- and plus there was an operational pace to keep up here of moving these persons that were permitted to leave Zepa and to try to maintain both the pace and to ensure that it was done under maximum conditions possible of maintaining security and any sort of -- maintaining any humanitarian standard. So we were under quite tremendous stress, and we were also aware of the context in which this happened, that this isn't just a logistics operation of moving some people from one place to another. This is an operation in which a population is being expelled from their homes in war time and this -- we were quite aware of the context in which we were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at this packet of reports, and this is 65 ter 2438. And just to give Your Honours a quick look, this is just the cover, the old cover, and this is what we plan to replace. As we can see, the Defence has the new and improved version already and will have the English available and obviously the tab numbers here refer to the physical tabs that are on the packet of memoranda and reports. So what I'd like to do is go to page 3 in e-court. And then the next page. And this is also page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What we have here is a 20 July, you can see the date, report from David Harland. And we see the abbreviation SCvAO. What does that stand for, sir? And please, again, pause, and I'll try to do my best as well.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: That stands for senior civil affairs officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We can see that the author is David Harland. And this is going to John Ryan. I think you described his position in your prior testimony. Can you just tell us what this acronym DSRSG/CAC is?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: DSRSG is deputy special representative of the Secretary-General. CAC, civil affairs co-ordinator. Or, chief civil affairs, I believe civil affairs co-ordinator. Even now I'm a little hazy, but in any event it means the head of the civil affairs operation in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see the subject is: "Meeting on Prisoners Exchange and Evacuation of Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see it's basically the same information, the from and to lines here. And it makes reference to a meeting at 2.00 in the afternoon at the Sarajevo airport. It was attended by Amor Masovic. And can you tell the Trial Chamber what his position was in July of 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: At that time he was a representative from, again, what is referred to then as the Bosnian side on prisoner exchange matters. As far as I recall, that was his portfolio. I don't recall that he had other portfolio than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It says Lieutenant Colonel Indjic represented the Serbs, and can you tell the Trial Chamber who Lieutenant Colonel Indjic was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: For UN purposes he was a liaison officer, but his portfolio might have been somewhat different from Mr. Masovic in that he might have had other duties, not just prisoner exchange duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at the next paragraph it refers to four hours of talks, and an agreement in principle that there should be an all-for-all exchange. And before we go any further, in your experience, sir, what is meant by an all-for-all exchange? Just generally speaking, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Having -- clearly I was not in attendance at this meeting. I was in Zepa, if I correctly understand the time and date, but I had been present in other such meetings and my understanding was all-for-all meant all those held by one side in exchange are for all those held by the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we read further on it says Harland reports here that: "No final agreement was made because the Bosnians were not satisfied that the Serbs had accounted for all the prisoners taken in the assault on the Srebrenica enclave. The Serbs agreed that they would try to produce a fuller reckoning of the Srebrenica prisoners in the next several hours." Can you tell the Trial Chamber how this issue that's reported on here by Mr. Harland, that the Bosnians were not satisfied that the Serbs had accounted for the prisoners taken in the fall of -- after the fall of Srebrenica, how that issue played out in your recollection during the time that you were involved in these Zepa events? Not just on the 20th, but going forward starting from this first meeting on the 20th at the airport. Understanding your caveat before that you were reporting as you could and so forth, but can you tell the Trial Chamber from your understanding of your communications with Harland and other people how, if at all, this issue played out during the course of these Zepa negotiations, whether it was at the airport or down in Zepa, and we'll get to more specific Zepa documents that you have more personal knowledge of later.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: With the understanding that when I was on the ground in Zepa, David Harland was not reporting to me. I might have had the opportunity to ask him some questions about the nature of the prisoner negotiations, but it would have been far more important for me and both my attention and his would have been more on the information from the ground in Zepa that I was passing to David. So with that caveat, I can say that in a general sense, the -- we were in general aware that the missing men from Srebrenica were an impediment to achieving a deal in the talks in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll look at one document in particular later, but can you tell the Trial Chamber for you personally, can you describe at what point you had concerns for the fate of the men of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: That -- my concerns about the fate of the men in Srebrenica date back to the time when I was in Tuzla receiving the buses of women from Srebrenica, and in the reference by the document you showed earlier, the case of the woman who tried to scale the barbed-wire fence because of a rumour she heard that perhaps the men from Srebrenica were somehow nearby in an adjacent location, and that example was just one that graphically drove home to me the fact that this is a burning issue. And it was one that I and my civil affairs colleague in Tuzla reported on and were mindful of, that the question of military-aged men being held captive in this context was even then for me, and this is without the knowledge of what is widely understood to have happened since, but even at that time was a major concern of mine and was present in my mind even at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could add -- if I could add that it was present in my mind while we were on the ground in Zepa with respect to the fate of what might happen to the men in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a procedural reality that we need to deal with, Mr. President, as I am sure it hasn't been lost on the Trial Chamber, this is a packet of individual reports, so we did not split this packet up into 18 separate exhibits. It is listed with one 65 ter number. Some of these documents do have separate 65 ter numbers which we could tender. We can find out for the record whether the Defence has objections to each of these reports, and if there are none then we can tender the entire packet at the appropriate time, or we can wait until later and then deal with that, but I think it may be worth the time to simply take report by report, just find out whether there are any objections on the record to an individual report, and if there are none we can note that, and at the end of the day when we've gone through all the reports in the packet then we can tender it. Otherwise, we'll have to go back and discuss every single report out of context months from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's a good proposal to do that. For a better understanding of the whole package we saw at the beginning the front page, that was related to the Popovic case. Did I understand you correctly that you will replace that page by another page in relation to this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. President, with this case's 65 ter numbers and caption and relevant information on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender the report in tab 1 of 2438 which, and I can just read the ERNs, is R043-3803 to R043-3804.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please check the number again, this is the ERN number, if that is the correct one which we have on the record because your reading was quite fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. That's R043-3803 to R043-3804.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I understood it correctly, we are talking about the number of reports bearing one in the same 65 ter number. Maybe this is simply a matter of proper organisation of work, but I think that we should make things easier for us, so if we are going to tender this whole package, it should also bear one number. If it is already a one single exhibit in e-court it should have one number.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think as I tried to explain, I'm to some degree engaging in a small fiction. I'm tendering this tab with the understanding that there will be no ruling of ultimate admissibility, we are simply seeking whether there's an a objection to this tab for the time being, this particular report within this one exhibit, so I'm not expecting -- or even though I said we tender tab 1, I guess I can ask are there objections to tab 1 so we can note that for the record, because I don't think the Prosecution's intention is not to tender this whole packet today unless we authenticate it through the witness but -- and if we do then I will tender the entire packet, but I think there may be one or two reports which we'll use with somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is always open for a party to use it -- tender an admitted document with another witness. I understood, Mr. Gajic, that it would be -- the Defence would be in favour to have the whole package admitted as one document, and I think this is quite reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's my -- that was, I thought, my communicated intention was to ultimately tender this as one document, but in the meantime I think it will be more useful in terms of our time to deal with these reports one by one on a case by case rather than coming back to this document after the witness has left the stand and then have to deal with them out of context. We've just discussed the document, we can get the Defence's views on the document, whether they object to it or not, we can note it for the record whether there's an objection or not, and then when we're done we can tender the whole collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you are able to do that in the two hours you have indicated for examination-in-chief. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one clarification about our position. We are, of course, going to object the admittance of any documents which were not authenticated by this witness. I was a little while ago talking simply about the procedure of tendering, so now if we have one 65 ter number and then we say tab 1 is exhibit such and, tab 2 is exhibit such and such, I think that this may result in a confusion. They should be better organised, the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many documents are in this package?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There are 18 tabs, Mr. President, within this packet which again has been organised for the convenience of all parties, so they are in one place in a particular order with an index so that they are more easily manageable. I don't see how it helps anybody to chop it up into 18 separate 65 ter number and ultimately exhibit numbers when we've got one clean packet that everybody can refer to and which frankly we are going to be referring to by e-court page number, so it's not going to help anybody to have it come in as a separate exhibit which will be a one or two page document where we are going to be dealing with this on the record in the e-court version which is paginated numerically as one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you should proceed and try to get through these documents. We can see if they will be authenticated by this witness and after that we shall discuss the matter if the document in a whole can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, with respect to tab 1, the question is whether the -- I think the Defence has any objection to this particular tab. And the authentication. If they have an issue of authentication for this document, let's deal with it now rather than having to wait until some other time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May there be peace in this house and may this witness spend his time comfortably here in this courtroom and may God's will be done in these proceedings. Now, if the witness does know something about these documents that were listed under 65 ter, then I would have no objection because we trust that the -- we trust this witness and we believe his words, so that would be all that I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may go to page 21 in e-court, please, and we'll see that this is tab 4. If we could go to the next page in both, it's going to be page -- yes, next page in both the B/C/S and the English. We can see here same format as the prior report, the date now is 21 July 1995. And the subject is: "Zepa Negotiations, Report Number 3."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, Your Honours, the previous report, "Zepa Negotiations Number 2" has already been admitted and is part of the packet, but we don't need to go over old ground so we are just skipping ahead to number 3. If we could go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the clarity of the record, if you say it was already admitted, under which number? Do you have the P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Bear with me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If not at the moment, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll get back to you, I'll move on, thank you. If we could go to the next page, please. We can see that this refers to another meeting at the airport about the exchange of prisoners and the evacuation of Zepa. And Mr. Harland reports that those negotiations collapsed. The meeting collapsed because the Serbs refused to give any names of prisoners taken when they overran Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've already told us about the concerns that you had and the general concerns of which you were aware that the Bosniaks had about the fate of the men from Srebrenica and role that that played in these negotiations, so let's go to the next page if we could save a little bit of time. The date of this document was the 21st of July, sir. And were you back in Sarajevo by that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we see here an assessment that's provided by Mr. Harland. And in creating these reports and these assessments, can you describe what your role was without necessarily referring to a particular report, but generally speaking, can you tell the Trial Chamber what your role was, how did you and Mr. Harland work together with respect to his assessments as they are reflected in this report and others that we'll see?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: David and I worked closely together over this period, and I'm sure that we discussed and exchanged views about what we thought was happening, and I'm sure I shared my views and my own assessment with David. That being said, as the report purports, and you see his signature there, it is his report in the end, but David and I would have had close conversation about this and about the approach and our views were largely consonant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at the risk of asking you to sound immodest perhaps, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether your understanding was that Mr. Harland relied on your consultation and observations when you would discuss these matters?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I -- it's here not a question for the Court being modest or not, I want to be very accurate for the Court. David Harland was then and remains a very capable, highly capable, highly intelligent, and at that point he and I both were highly experienced in Bosnia, so it would be inaccurate to suggest that I was the source for David. David was perfectly capable of arriving at an assessment, an accurate one, a very accurate one on his own. At the same time, did I contribute and share views and did he and I discuss things in an open and very close way? Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this assessment, and let's just jump down to the second paragraph, he says: "It is unlikely that there will be any evacuation of Zepa in the next day or two. Most likely, the Serbs will now intensify their military pressure on the pocket in an effort to force the local military commander to accept Serb terms. This might take several days given that they seem reluctant to commit their infantry until the Bosnians are broken by bombardment." Can you tell the Trial Chamber to what extent during this period of time when this assessment was made you shared the assessment that's expressed here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I believe I shared this assessment following our return from Zepa, from the first time we were at Zepa and there when we saw the resumption of bombardment, or heard, I should say heard, the resumption of bombardment to be very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was your assessment that this bombardment was targeting the Muslim military only or the Muslim military as well as the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: With artillery and with a location as small as Zepa was, and with the experience of having been in Sarajevo, I don't think we would have anticipated that there would have been much of a distinction between civilian and military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us a little bit more what you mean when you say, "I don't think we would have anticipated that there would have been much of a distinction between civilian and military targets." Are you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: When we heard -- pausing. When we heard -- for example, when artillery was used in that context, that we were there present, Viktor and I were present for, I don't think we were under any impression that those shells were being directed purely towards, for example, a military barracks if one even existed in Zepa. This was a small village and the tactics of the war were such, for example, in Sarajevo that bombardment was regularly aimed at targets that were clearly non-military in nature. Military at times, targets, sure might be purely military, but it was a regular feature of this war that artillery, those who had it would use it in -- towards -- in addition to non-military objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see, I think we are at the new break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed we are. We must have our break now and resume in half an hour at 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to note for the record, I believe that the exhibit issues that we were dealing with earlier have been resolved and all parties have access to all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And also to follow-up on that tab 2 I referred to which had been previously admitted, that has been admitted but it's awaiting an assignment of its P number, so I can't give you that right now either unfortunately, but ... And to give you the -- some idea of the timing, I've cut a number of exhibits from my examination given my estimate. I may need to exceed it slightly, but I have reduced my examination-in-chief to the bare essentials, I think, and I'm working towards that two hours as closely as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we go on to the next document, Mr. President, with respect to tab 4 which is the document we just looked at, again if we could find out from the Defence whether they have any objections to this document being admitted as part of 2438 when the time comes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you in a position to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence does not object to the admittance of any of the documents that relate to the responsibility or that can speak to the responsibility of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may go to page 25 in the document, and we'll see that that's tab 5, and that's page 23 in the B/C/S version. Go to the next page, please, in both versions. I apologise, there is no translation for this one yet, so if we can just focus on the English. We can see that this is another same format as the prior reports we saw. This one is dated the 22nd of July from Mr. Harland and it's subject is Zepa negotiations and this is report 4 of the series. If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see that it deals with a meeting between Mr. Harland and General Gobillard in which Mr. Harland suggests that the UN offer the parties a radical demilitarisation proposal, an idea proposed by Ed Joseph three days ago. Do you recall testifying about that demilitarisation proposal in the last trial, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page. Let's focus on the assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again this is dated the 22nd of July. Are you back in Sarajevo at this point or are you down in Zepa; do you recall, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: From my understanding of the sequence, I think I'm back in Sarajevo at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we focus on the assessment, Mr. Harland writes: "Our proposal for the total demilitarisation of Zepa remains a long shot. It is true that the Serbs are reluctant to attack the Zepa pocket until they have completely worn down its population. On the other hand, it is hard to imagine that they would accept any arrangement that would leave Zepa in Bosnian hands. I imagine that they will continue to make life in Zepa as miserable as possible for the local population until - demoralised by the assault and abandoned by the international community - they accept the 'evacuation' option being prosed by the Serbs." Now, sir, my first question is, in July of 1995 did you share this assessment that the Serbs were reluctant to attack until they had completely worn down its population?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Without being 100 per cent pinning me down to whether on that day did I have that assessment, without being microscopically precise about that, I would say yes, that I was aware as were my colleagues that the Serbs were reluctant to do an infantry assault in Zepa because of the likelihood that they would take substantial casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And these references to the population and the local population, are those references to military, Muslim military forces, Muslim civilians only, both, or what is your understanding when Mr. Harland refers to its population and the local population, who or what is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Again, it's David's document so he is the one who would be categorical about what he meant, but my understanding is it would be both, both the civilian and military population.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience down there in Zepa during this time, how was the civilian population being made miserable and worn down as indicated here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Isolation, deprivation, and then artillery bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Finally, we see here that the word "evacuation," if you look at the paragraph in the assessment, the last sentence, the word "evacuation" is in quotations. Can you tell the Trial Chamber why the word "evacuation" is in quotation marks?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Repeating my caveat that this is David's report, I would surmise David and I would probably have shared this view that evacuation is so-called in this context but really what we are talking about is expulsion. In other words, the forced expulsion of the population, not a evacuation because of as one would do in the case of a flood or a -- some natural disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we are done with this document, Mr. President. The Prosecution would seek the Defence's position on the admissibility of this document as part of Exhibit 2438.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is your previous comment also valid for this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
