utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, Your Honour. It is valid for this document as well. Whatever is accepted by the witness will be accepted by us because we know that he wouldn't agree or accept -- agree to or accept something that he hadn't seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead, please, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could go to page 35 in the English, and that will be page 27 in the B/C/S. We can see we are at tab 7 for the record. If we could just advance one page in each and I'll just note that we don't have a translation of the fax cover page that we've seen on a couple of these. We do have a translation of the substantive report that we'll be looking at, so just for the time being I'm going to note that we can see here this is a similar format report from David Harland. The date is the 25th of July, 1995, and this is subject: "Zepa Negotiations 6." And if we can go to the next page in the English only and stay where we are in the B/C/S. We can see Harland reporting that he received a message from the Ukrainians indicating that the local Bosnians had accepted the terms of surrender and evacuation of Zepa and that he asked Mr. Bezruchenko and yourself to travel immediately there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My first question is, is this the second trip that you testified about in Popovic and that we've already heard a little bit about today, that you took down to Zepa? Is that what's reflected here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to direct your attention to the third paragraph where he says that: "At 11.00 a.m. Bezruchenko called Harland and told Harland that he had he seen the elements of an agreement signed by Rajko Kusic and Hamdija Torlak." The question is simply, do you recall that happening?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I have a hazy memory, but I have no reason to doubt the accuracy of this record, of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this reference to Lukavica, what is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Lukavica barracks were the Serb military presence nearest Sarajevo where we would have frequent meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Serb Sarajevo I think even now they refer to that side as.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution again would seek the Defence's position on tab 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that the response will be the same, otherwise the Defence will object.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I'll try to save time and just keep going. If we could see page 54, please, in e-court, and this will be page 37 in the B/C/S. We don't have a translation of this one, unfortunately. And if we could go to the next page, we see we are at tab 10 of the document, just for the record. This is another Harland report dated the 26th of July, the subject is: "Zepa Negotiations Number 9." If we could just turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a reference to another meeting at the Sarajevo airport, and if we look at the assessment, Mr. Harland reports that: "The Bosnians, recognising the extreme weakness of their negotiating position, seemed to have accepted that they will not get back any significant number of prisoners taken in the Srebrenica operation (these prisoners account for upwards of 90 per cent of all the prisoners held by the Serbs). The Bosnians will not agree, however, that the men of Zepa should ever fall into Serb hands." My question to you, sir, is let's locus on that last sentence, the Bosnian's position that the men of Zepa should never fall into Serb hands. To what degree did that position figure into the discussions that you were part of or aware of during your involvement in the Zepa events in July of 1995? If you can't remember a specific meeting or conversation, that's okay, but can you give the Trial Chamber a sense of in general to what extent this position was evident to you or not.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I'll answer in two parts. First in terms of the sequence here, we should bear in mind that I am now back in Zepa. So my awareness of evolution or non-evolution of the parties' positions is limited, so I'm not clear now exactly on what I knew relayed to me in Zepa at the time. So there's that limitation on my awareness of the on-going developments in those negotiations and discussions in Sarajevo. That being said, my own awareness was that of course that this was important not only for what is termed there, again I'm using the term as it's used in David's report, "Bosnians," you've used Bosniak, but for the report we at that time were using the term "Bosnians," but this was something that was of concern to us even, I would say, independently of the Bosnian position. In other words we, and I know myself in my own mind, had a concern about what would happen to the men of Zepa and what modalities there would be to ensure that they would -- if an all-for-all exchange were agreed upon, what modalities there would be to effect their safe transfer from that region to across the lines into the Bosnian-controlled territory. So I think I was generally aware of that position but even independently from any position on the -- even if there were no expressed concern, I know I had that concern myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was that concern based upon, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: That concern was based upon three years of experience in the war and the particular recent memory of the situation in Srebrenica where we did not know the fate of the men of Srebrenica, and where that was a giant question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's move to page 60. And for the record, that was again tab 10 that we just looked at. And we are now looking at tab 12. This will be page 42 in the B/C/S, please, and there is a B/C/S translation for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move on, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, I wonder if you can assist me to understand, at page 52, line 19 to 21, you are talking of the forced expulsion of the population and not an evacuation, and you say in explaining -- you say because of -- it's not a flagged or a natural disaster, in this particular I have a question. Then in the correspondence and the various documents that we have there is frequent reference to evacuation of the population, so in your assessment at what point then does evacuation become forced expulsion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Very fair question. I would have to see in the documents the reference to evacuation to know whether that term was being used in the context of a proposal by the Serbs, in other words, that was the term that they used and was reflecting that, or whether it was reflecting an independent use of the term by David Harland. So I would respectfully have to look and see what it was. There was the reference to the assessment of David Harland where evacuation was put in quotation marks and that I explained the purpose of those was because it's so-called as they say in Serbian [B/C/S spoken] so-so called evacuation. We were -- I should put you at ease, Judge, that we were under no dilemma whatsoever that this was a forced expulsion. I should just simply put the Chamber at ease about that. There was no -- absolutely no dilemma, no debate whatsoever. We understood what this was and I don't think that it was not even a subject of debate, discussion, or dilemma whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. I've asked my question in the context of what is at page 53 today's testimony, lines 16 to 20, and I think it's Mr. Thayer paraphrasing a question where he says: "We can see Harland reporting that he received a message from the Ukrainians indicating that the local Bosnians had accepted the terms of surrender and evacuation of Zepa and that he asked Mr. B and yourself to travel there," in that context. I have asked my question in the context of those words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge, that's very helpful for me. And in my understanding would simply be reflecting the -- what it seems to be to me is the Ukrainians are reflecting the use of that term in this agreement that has been made and that that's what's being reflected in the report. That would be my understanding. The larger point here, though, I'm trying to convey to the Chamber that there was no debate or impression or I might even use the term, if the Chamber will permit me, illusion that this was anything other than a forced expulsion and that not anyone that I would know in the UN side would have any impression that this was somehow analogous to evacuating people for their safety as one would do in the nature of a flood or an earthquake. If that answers your question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any time then in war when there is an evacuation or is it just in floods, in natural disaster that there can be an evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that -- I suppose that there could be circumstances in the context of a war where one might -- we see today a good example in Libya. We see civilian populations being evacuated, British, Germans, others being evacuated from there because of the unrest and the risk there and what is a conflict, if not a war, a conflict in Libya. So, Judge, you are quite right, those circumstances do exist. My impression is that that was simply not what we were confronting at that time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Okay. If we could go to the next page in both versions, please. Again, this is tab 12 for the record. And I note for the record with respect to the prior transcript which has now been received at page 14316, this document was used by the Beara team in its cross-examination but was not admitted at that point, but it's the same document, just for the clarity of the record. What we have here, as we can see, is another report, the same format, the date is 28 July, 1995, from Mr. Harland, and its subject is: "Zepa Negotiations Number 11." If we can go to the next page in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see in the very first paragraph Mr. Harland is reporting that he spoke with you at about 0800 hours that morning on the 28th and that you had spoken to General Mladic about Avdo Palic. The report here indicates that you told Mr. Harland that Mladic had said that Palic is dead when you asked him about what happened to Palic. And I believe you clarified this in your prior testimony, and this is at transcript page 4207, but just briefly, if you would, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether your recollection is that Mladic actually told you that Palic was dead or did he tell something else, do you think is possible?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Let me say that this would inform my entire testimony here and it might be interesting for the Chamber that there are certain things that I have vivid memories of and other things that I have, where 16 years later, almost 16 years later, the memories are much more hazy. I have a vivid memory of the efforts that Viktor and I made after Colonel Palic was seized by Serb military personnel from the UNPROFOR compound and we were eye-witness to this, including the immediate pursuit to try to locate what happened to him. What I recall is that we didn't see Mladic immediately, but I believe the next day I had a radio conversation with Mladic, this is what my memory is, from our location down in the village and to his location where he was above, and it was at that time that I understood that he had said Palic had been killed, and then subsequent to that what I recall is that Viktor and I saw later Mladic's interpreter and asked her to confirm that he had said that and my memory is that she, in some ways, had confirmed that. What is a possibility to me is that there could have been either a mistranslation or misunderstanding where it's possible that Mladic might have said in Serbian "pobjegao" instead of something that might have come across at "ubio" or "ubio ga" something like that. It might have been "pobjegao," in other words, he might have said he had escaped. So that is a possibility that remains. So that's my recollection of that communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the next paragraph on this page, second paragraph. Harland reports that: "Ed also stated that he had met with General Tolimir yesterday ..." so that would be the 27th of July, "... and Tolimir had told him that the Serbs would accept an arrangement under which the Bosnian fighters in the hills could be transported by UNPROFOR to central Bosnia as a part of the all-for-all exchange deal being negotiated at Sarajevo airport." My question to you is, given what Mr. Harland is reporting here that you told him, did it appear to you that General Tolimir was knowledgeable about what was going on at the Sarajevo airport or not given that he is referring to the negotiations there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I would say yeah, based on the conversation that we had that it was certainly apparent that General Tolimir was aware that these negotiations were proceeding, I can't specify to what precision his information was or how specifically he had awareness of where those negotiations were, but in general terms he was -- the context would have been one in which he would have been aware of the -- of those negotiations and what the general positions were of the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm moving through my two hours, Mr. President. I think at this point I have just three more documents. I've cut the rest from my list and if I could have a couple of more minutes to spend with Mr. Joseph on these three documents I'd be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go to page 64, please, in the English and this would be page 46 in the B/C/S. Again we don't have a translation of the cover page, the fax cover page, but we do have a translation of the substantive memo of the report. So for the record we can see we are at tab 13. If we could go to the next page, please. We can see here in the English only it's dated the 29th of July, 1995, another report in the same format from Mr. Harland, the subject is: "Zepa Negotiations 12." And if we could go to the next page in both versions, please. We can see the same information about the date, 29 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I want to draw your attention to is on the next page, if we could go to the next page in both versions - the middle paragraph where it says "also during the afternoon" we can see Mr. Harland reports: "Also during the afternoon, I received a message from Ed Joseph in Zepa who indicated that the Serbs were apparently planning to seise a number of Bosnian fighters, ('war criminals') regardless of what agreement was reached. He noted that the Serbs seemed to be using UNPROFOR to entice the Bosnians to give up their weapons, and were perhaps using UNPROFOR to give the Bosnians a false sense of security." If you would, can you just focus on that one paragraph, I know it's got a couple of points to it, but if you could take a moment and just explain to the Trial Chamber what you were communicating to Mr. Harland in this conversation you had with him that he is memorialising in this report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I recall a conversation I had with General Mladic in which I asked him was he going to permit -- if there were an agreement in Sarajevo, was he going to permit the Bosnian men, Bosnian as we called then, today we would probably say Bosniak, to continue on, and continue on their way. And the reason I asked this was because I had concerns in this regard, and as I recall he said oh, yes, we will let them go except for the war criminals, and I took that to mean that General Mladic and his forces would exercise quite a bit of discretion as to whom they would actually -- of the men of Zepa whom they would actually permit to leave and whom they would not. And that discretion might be very wide indeed. That's what was the way I read and understood that. And that would have been what I -- in all likelihood this is what David is referring to. The second part with using UNPROFOR to entice Bosnians to give up their weapons, false sense of security, I think here reflects my own skepticism, and I'm sure David sharing that and aware of that, of the actual limitations of UNPROFOR to truly secure populations and number of examples of that inability or failure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let's focus on the men of military age who are implicit, I think, in this paragraph, correct me if I'm wrong, when you say that you were expecting that the VRS would exercise wide discretion in who they characterised as, to use the terms in the document, war criminals. What concerns, if any, did you you have about what would happen to those men who General Mladic told you would be characterised as war criminals? And if you had concerns, what were those concerns based on?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I would have concerns as to -- as to their safety. I would -- those were the concerns that I had, as to whether they would -- had been promised freedom, would actually see that. At that time we did not know about the developments in Srebrenica, but as I said, the fact that so many men were still missing was certainly something that was quite present in my mind, and we also -- I understood that from the Serb perspective these were -- these were fighters, these were their enemy, and to permit a sizeable number of their enemy to continue across the lines only to then be re-engaged against them, I did not -- I was not convinced that the Serbs would simply permit that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to press you just a little bit. When you say you have -- you said you had concerns as to their safety. I mean, war is a dangerous time, that area is a dangerous place just to drive a car. When you are talking about safety, what are you referring to, sir, if you could be more specific?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I have to be careful here because we are talking about -- I'm trying to be as precise for this Chamber as I can be about my awareness at the time. The problem, of course, is its a matter of record of what transpired in Srebrenica, so I'm trying to be as precise as I possibly can to disregard what we've all come to know transpired in Srebrenica from what my state was at the time. I had -- I had a great amount of fear that at least some of these men might well be killed. So I had a fear that they -- some of them might well be executed. Did I -- at that time was I convinced or worried that all of them would be executed? I don't know. I don't know necessarily that I was, but I had certainly a concern that some of them would be in mortal danger if they fell into General Mladic's control.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's move to page 69 in e-court for the last two documents. This is tab 14 for the record. We don't have a translation unfortunately in B/C/S, so if we could just focus on the next page in English, please. We can see it's also dated the 29th of July, another report in the same format from Mr. Harland, the subject here is: "Zepa Negotiations Report Number 12." And I think everybody will agree shortly that this is a typo and it should be 13 as we'll see from the next page. If we could go to the next page, please. We can see here the subject is: "Negotiations on Zepa, Report 13." What I'd like to do is go to the next page and focus on the portion that involves yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Harland is reporting on a conversation that he had with Mr. Bezruchenko and then you. We see in the paragraph just before the assessment, Mr. Harland reports: "Ed then spoke and repeated that General Tolimir had told General Gobillard that UNPROFOR could evacuate the men of Zepa directly if the Bosnians would accept an all-for-all prisoner exchange." My question is casting your memory back to this time, did you draw any conclusions at all about General Tolimir's intentions from this conversation that you had with him where he expressed what's being reported here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Could you clarify the word "intentions" please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure. Did you take what General Tolimir told you at face value, let me ask it that way?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I can say right now without reference to other documents or -- I can say I know that from our standpoint and from my standpoint we were looking, and always as UN personnel, were always exploring and looking for any possibility of striking an agreement that could save lives and alleviate a stand-off and so -- but precisely an inference as to a specific intention, I don't know from that paragraph if I can say. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, and I'll pause just for a second: On the 29th of July, where were the men of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: From our knowledge that we had, they were above us hiding in these dense forests, in these steep hills and dense forests.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And did UNPROFOR or the VRS have any custody or control over those men at that point?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: No, we did not. Neither we nor did the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You just testified that General Mladic told you that they would permit all of the men from Zepa to simply walk to free territory, and you've told us about your concerns for their safety. So my question is, when General Tolimir told you that these men could be evacuated directly, if they accepted an all-for-all, was that part of the context in which you had this conversation or not or if you can't remember that's fine too, just trying to get your best recollection of what you -- let me put it this way, to use the phrase "took away" from that conversation with General Tolimir? Not asking you to try to read his mind. You don't have that degree, but just asking you what you took away.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Absolutely. You have to please understand, and if the Chamber would understand, that there is an obligation on our part doing in effect mediation to reflect the formal position that a senior responsible party like General Tolimir conveyed to us. So the fact that he conveyed that position we had an obligation, regardless of whether we felt it ultimately credible or not, but that this reflected in any event a position that he as a senior and authoritative interlocutor would tell us. That being said, if you ask separately, was I somehow assured that, unlike with General Mladic, that General Tolimir having said this that oh, that that would somehow assure that these men would arrive safely, my answer to that is no. My answer to that is my same preoccupation for the ultimate safety of those men remain the same with what General Tolimir had told me or and what General Mladic had told me, that in either case had such a deal -- my mind was concerned that in fact they would come to an agreement and that how we would, as UNPROFOR, create the modalities so that these men would not be snatched in the midst of it, and that apprehension and preoccupation applied with equality whether with respect to General Mladic or General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The last document I wanted to use is actually on the Defence's list of exhibits, it's 65 ter 7208. I'll stop here, Mr. President, and if the Defence picks up that document then fine, if not, that's fine too, and that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that you are tendering the whole package 65 ter 2438?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's a little premature right now, Mr. President. There are a couple that I cut out that we'll use with another witness, so we'll just let it lie for now and we'll tender it at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, you may commence your cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to everyone yet again. May there be peace in this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings and not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the witness again. I'd like him to answer my questions as he remembers them and based on his knowledge, not on assumptions. After all, I think that the Prosecutor did seek some speculative answers from the witness, what would have happened had the case been such and such, and I will not venture there. I would like us to stick to the facts. Let's start from the last document, page 66, line 5. It says, the Prosecutor told you, you said that General Mladic said that everyone should cross over to free territory and were guarantees any different when Tolimir told you this, and then you said on page 66 that it didn't matter really whether it was General Mladic or I that told you this, you felt preoccupied for these men and you wanted to see the agreement carried out without the Muslims being taken away by the Serbian Army. Please tell me this, do you recall, did most of the combatants, those wounded who were really in combat, and were known to be in combat, were wounded, were they allowed to leave without any conditions and based on the agreements that I gave to you and Palic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should switch off your microphone, Mr. Tolimir, during the discussion with your legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, let me return the wishes here about the proceedings, and let me state that; that is, the answer to the question were the seriously wounded permitted to be evacuated, the answer to that is yes, they were. This was a subject, this was part of the agreement, and it was respected. There was -- there were specific conditions applied. There was a doctor from the Serb army and an UNPROFOR doctor, and the two of them examined the men and determined which ones were in a serious condition such that they had to be medivaced out and I believe ICRC was there, so the answer to the question is yes, those -- those men were evacuated, those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please let us look in e-court, document D55 page 29 in Serbian, let's look at that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll read the relevant paragraph to see what the number of the wounded was really since you couldn't remember it. And I'm quoting: "On the 25th of July, UNPROFOR started the evacuation from Zepa. The French battalion Sector Sarajevo sent a convoy to Zepa for the evacuation of the wounded. On the following morning, the convoy returned to Sarajevo with 151 people, 29 were seriously wounded and immediately treated by the medical staff at the Sarajevo hospital. Around midnight, around 1.000 people were evacuated by the VRS with their own buses and they were take to the confrontation line near Kladanj," and so on and so forth, end of quote. This is my question: Based on this, is it not obvious that the Army of the Republika Srpska fulfilled the terms of the agreement without placing any subsequent conditions that had not been previously included into the agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, for the record and for the sake of the witness, it would be helpful if you could indicate from which document you are reading and which document is it we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is Viktor Bezruchenko's report and he was with Mr. Joseph in Zepa. Upon their return, he drew up this report for the purposes of the Prosecution as their witness, so in other words, it's Mr. Bezruchenko's own report; therefore, a gentleman who was -- who went on this mission together with Mr. Joseph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I would answer with three points. I say three so I remember to address all three. The narrow answer to the question put to me is yes. The seriously wounded, as is reported in what General Tolimir has referred to as Mr. Bezruchenko's report, is correct, that the seriously wounded were evacuated. The people, it says "people," but we are talking about women and children there, were evacuated, and that is true. Because the question was posed to me in the context of my view about what would have happened to the men who were hiding in the hills, I can tell you that the fact that these seriously wounded were evacuated and the fact that the women and the children were evacuated, neither now nor then at all affected my apprehension for the safety of those men and this would be borne out when we discussed the question of the lightly wounded men who my understanding was were not permitted safe -- who were given permission to me to pass but were in fact seized by VRS shortly after they exited Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will come back to that question later as to why they were kept and subsequently exchanged. Let's leave that for later. Let's look at document D51, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have the document before us entitled "Agreement on the disarmament of the Able-bodied Population in the Zepa Enclave." We can see that it was agreed to on the 24th of July, 1995, between Rajko Kusic who was the commander of the VRS Brigade and Hamdija Torlak on the other who was the president of the executive committee of Zepa in the presence of the UNPROFOR representative Semjon Dudnjik. Let's look at item 1 which says that a cease-fire should be forthwith established between the warring parties. So my question for you is: Was a cease-fire immediately established in view of your arrival on the 24th when, as you say, you came across those women in the centre? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Two answers to this question. The first is, yes, there appeared to be no firing, and a cease-fire, yes, did appear to be in place in there, yes. And part two to my answer is this agreement was not something that we thought we were implementing. I think there was reference to another document in which I had raised to General Smith the question of the validity of a local civilian conveying a surrender of military forces, and I had raised the question according to laws of war as to whether that had effect. And for example, this paragraph 5 that Commander Palic shall start disarming his units immediately. This is something that this document and such a paragraph, this had absolutely no bearing on what we were doing there. We were there to, yes, an understanding that a cease-fire was in place, but we were there to effect the -- this transport as safely and securely and humanely as we could of initially the civilian population and perhaps in time of the male population as well, whether they be military or civilian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so there's no confusion on the record, and I don't think there will be any dispute from the Defence on this, I think the witness's testimony has been clear and consistent that he arrived for the second time on the 25th of July, not the 24th as General Tolimir may have misspoken in his question. So I just wanted to clarify that for the record, again I don't think there's any dispute but just so we have a clear record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness can help us with this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, for that I refer to the documents. And I believe the documents do show that Viktor and I returned on the 25th. I believe that that's the case. Again, relying with reference to documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, as soon as you feel that I misstate certain facts in relation to either documents or your knowledge of them, please draw my attention to that, I am not opposed to that at all. Let's look at item of the agreement which reads that: "The civilian and able-bodied population of Zepa shall assemble around the UNPROFOR base in Zepa which will be a sign to the army that the units under the command of Avdo Palic have accepted a truce and will not try to take advantage of it." When you got there, did you see around the UNPROFOR base women, children, and civilians? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at item 5 that you've just referred to, that Avdo Palic shall commence disarming his units and that all the weapons shall be handed over to the VRS representatives in the UNPROFOR base this Zepa. Was it realistic, the request put forth by the Muslims, that the army should be disarmed, the army under the command of Avdo Palic, and that the weapons be surrendered to the UNPROFOR base? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Perhaps the -- I was not listening to you -- to the accused in Serbian, but I think there might have been a mistake perhaps in the translation. Is -- "was a Serb demand." You said was -- it was translated as "a Muslim demand," but you were asking whether the Serb demand was reasonable. Is that your question, General?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to avoid any confusion, this is an agreement in which both sides agree on several things, among them that Avdo Palic shall commence disarmament of his units, and that all weapons should be handed over to the representatives of the VRS in the UNPROFOR base in Zepa. So is this one of the stipulations of this agreement agreed to by both parties? It certainly wasn't only the view of the Serbian side because if the Muslims didn't agree with that, they could have said it and there would be no agreement then. So you took part in the negotiations and in the signing of this agreement, do you consider that this was a one-sided view or that this was indeed an agreement signed by both parties? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: Thank you for restating and clarifying the question. I need to be very, very clear for the Chamber. I was not present for the signing nor was I present and nor did I or Viktor have any role whatsoever in the negotiations for this document. Again, if you can see, it's dated 24 July and we returned to Zepa on the 25th. These were presumably, not something I know, but presumably these were discussions, General, that your side had with these -- this civilian leader and I think there were other civilian leaders including the hodza who then went missing. Then -- so we were not witnesses or privy to this document. That's number one. I don't want to speak too fast for the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Then the other point I want to underscore is that we -- I do not recall us in any respect thinking that we were implementing or assisting in the implementation of this document. It was -- we were there as I said, to as humanely and safely as possible to be in a co-ordinating role for the transport of this population. And as I restated, there was a question even then, General, that General Smith understood and when I conveyed it to him about the validity of this, so that -- that's all being said. Now, if you want my opinion on the Serb position, if you want my opinion on whether it was reasonable to ask for the Muslim side to disarm, in the context, this was a common demand as we know. This had been done in Srebrenica back with General Morillon in 1993 and there was -- this was a frequent and common demand was demilitarisation. So that's as far as I think I need to go on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now move the page upwards in e-court in both languages so that you could see the signatures in both languages. Thank you. Yes, English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There are no signatures in the English version, but you can here see, oh, yes, yes, on the second page you can see the signatures. And you can see that it was signed in the middle by Semjon Dudnjik. Can you tell the Trial Chamber who was Semjon Dudnjik and who was it who he represented during the drafting of this agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH
utterances.text: General Tolimir, wishing to truly be as helpful and co-operative as I can be, I can't tell you the answer to that question. As I said, I was not present for that, and I honestly and genuinely don't recall him. I do recall meet Mr. Torlak. I have a memory of him. It's possible I met Mr. Dudnjik, but I -- at this time I simply can't answer your question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment. One moment, please. Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar, can we please go back to the previous page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it should be enlarged a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There we go. Very well. Witness, today in the transcript on page 74, line 21, following a question that was put to you by General Tolimir, you said that it is quite usual that a party requests of another party to give back the -- render the weapons, surrender weapons, and this had already happened in 1993 while General Morillon was present. If we go back to the document that's on the screen, in the fifth paragraph - and I will translate it in French, but you can read it in English - it says: "Avdo Palic shall start disarming his units immediately and all the weapons should be handed over to the VRS representative in or of the Army of Republika Srpska at the UNPROFOR base in Zepa," end of quote. I would like to ask you the following: When we talk about those weapons, they were supposed to be handed over really to the representatives of the VRS or were they supposed to be handed over to the UNPROFOR? Can you therefore explain to us what was going on exactly with respect to the handing over of the weapons or, rather, by the demilitarisation of the enclave and the handing over of all the weapons of the UNPROFOR -- to the UNPROFOR. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Judge, I understand your question and what I can tell you is my understanding at the time was that there was no agreement on demilitarisation. I will -- [French spoken]. [Interpretation] And if you will, I will answer in French if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's very good. Thank you very much, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the point to emphasise here is that this provision on demilitarisation had no validity as far as the UN was concerned as far as I know. This was an agreement that a civilian representative who had -- civilian representatives who, my understanding is, had no authority to make commitments with respect to weapons had made, and I would presume - I'm going to underscore presume - that they made this agreement under great duress. The person in Zepa who had authority to agree to demilitarisation and surrender of weapons was Colonel Palic, who was the military commander. And he is the one who had the authority to make such a commitment. So -- and these -- I should add, Judge, for the context, you know, the UN was very familiar with agreements on demilitarisation and was not necessarily legally a party but a witness to such agreements and where the UN assumed obligations, it was with very careful awareness and involvement of UNPROFOR military, and that was not the case. This was, as I understand it, this was a document that was negotiated presumably under great duress by these civilian leaders trying to avert the continued bombardment of the town. And again, I can only emphasise to you that this provision about demilitarisation had -- it was not something that we were in the slightest implementing, monitoring, and I recall no discussion among UNPROFOR military either. This had simply no -- was not a -- valid in that sense. It conveyed an intention basically to give up but it was not -- this is not the document under which we were there in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to the first paragraph of this agreement, the top of this page. You see there: "On the 24th of July, 1995, the following agreement was reached between Rajko Kusic on one side and Hamdija Torlak on the other, in the presence of UNPROFOR representative Semjon Dudnjik." Perhaps that rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It does not ring a bell in terms of the -- thank you for pointing that out. It does not ring a bell in terms of that oh, now I remember this individual, I do not, but now what I presume is that this was the Ukrainian senior officer of the Ukrainian battalion, and that he was indeed present there. I can tell you though from my perspective as a UN civil affairs officer, we did not believe that we were there, or simply we did not have copies of this and were carrying out a provision, paragraphs of this. My memory of this is that we did not operate from this document as valid, notwithstanding the fact that there was this Ukrainian officer who was present. As I mentioned, this came up in a subsequent meeting when General Smith who was the overall commander was there as to whether or not this was valid, and I pointed out to General Smith that there's a question as to whether a civilian representative, Mr. Torlak, had authority to surrender weapons on behalf of his military which he did not. But you are quite right, Mr. President, absolutely, to point out that there presumably was an UNPROFOR representative. That being said, at no time do I recall us in any way carrying out, monitoring, accepting weapons or even really that being a matter of discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you any information about the authority of Mr. Dudnjik to sign such an agreement not as a part of the negotiations but on behalf of UNPROFOR to state his presence during this assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Completely valid question and I -- I simply do not know whether he had sought and obtained authorisation to witness this and to be a part of this. I don't know that and I'm sure if General Smith comes and testifies, he can attest to that. But this was not the document that we felt we were there to do, and again I don't recall any discussion and there would have been, and there of would have been. General Smith, I had spoke to him, he had personally originally directed us to go there, and we would have been made aware, as would the French military when they arrived that, oh, there would have been modalities set up for collecting these weapons and centralising them and those discussions. It was simply not an issue. We were focussed on this population transport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next question by Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Is it your position then that you don't recognise the validity of this agreement then or now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Judge, speaking about events that took place 16 years ago, I do not recall that we, Viktor Bezruchenko and I, the civil affairs officers who were there to co-ordinate the evacuation, I do not recall that we operated from the basis of this document at all. And it would be very unusual for us to go into such a situation where there were a document that was presumably what was to be implemented and then sort of disregard it and not pay attention to it. To the contrary, any time -- we took very seriously any agreements and documents, and I do not recall that we at all referred to such a document. We were there, we understood that there had been an agreement for the women and children to be evacuated. That's what we understood. And that there was a question about what would happen to the men was -- was up in the air, and with respect to their arms, I simply don't recall any reference to this whatsoever, Judge. I hope I've answered your question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: After this round of questions by the Judges, we have reached the time-limit of today. It is 7.00, we have to adjourn, and we ask you for your patience, you have to come back tomorrow in the afternoon. We are sitting in Courtroom III again at 2.15. Thank you very much. We adjourn.
